title: Random Forest
tagline: A forest of imperfect decision trees that together make surprisingly few mistakes.
what_it_is: Random Forest builds many decision trees, each trained on a random sample of the data and a random subset of features, then averages their predictions (regression) or takes a majority vote (classification). This randomness makes each tree different, so their combined errors cancel out.
key_points: It's bagging applied specifically to decision trees, plus random feature selection at each split.
Each tree sees a bootstrapped (random-with-replacement) sample of the training data.
Each split only considers a random subset of features — this decorrelates the trees.
Final prediction = majority vote (classification) or average (regression) across all trees.
Much less prone to overfitting than a single deep decision tree.
why_it_exists: A single decision tree grown deep enough will overfit — it memorizes the training data. Random Forest was built to keep the trees' flexibility while cancelling out their individual overfitting through averaging many decorrelated trees.
intuition: One decision tree is like one overconfident intern making a call based on limited experience. A random forest is 500 interns, each shown a different random slice of the company's history and a different random subset of the available reports, each making their own call independently. Vote them together and the group answer is far more reliable than any one intern's guess.

steps.title: Bootstrap sampling
steps.description: For each tree, randomly sample the training data with replacement to create a slightly different dataset.

steps.title: Random feature subset
steps.description: At every split in every tree, only consider a random subset of features rather than all of them.

steps.title: Grow trees independently
steps.description: Grow each tree fully (or to a max depth) without pruning — individual trees are allowed to overfit.

steps.title: Aggregate predictions
steps.description: Combine all trees' outputs by majority vote (classification) or averaging (regression).

when_to_use: Use as a strong, low-effort baseline for tabular classification or regression problems.
Use when you need feature importance estimates without much manual work.
Use when you want a model that's robust to outliers and doesn't need feature scaling.
when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need a fully interpretable, single decision path (use a single decision tree instead).
Do not expect it to extrapolate well on data far outside the training range — trees can only predict within seen value ranges.
Do not use for very high-dimensional sparse data like raw text — linear models or boosting often do better there.
common_mistakes: Setting n_estimators (number of trees) very high assuming it always helps — returns diminish and training slows down.
Not tuning max_depth or min_samples_leaf, leading to needlessly slow, memory-heavy trees.
Treating feature importance from Random Forest as causal — it only reflects predictive usefulness, not cause and effect.
ds_usage: One of the most common baseline models for structured/tabular data — used for churn prediction, credit scoring, fraud detection, and as a quick feature-importance check before building anything fancier.
